title: Sums and Differences of Cubes
trouble: Students write the middle sign of the trinomial the same as the binomial's sign.

blocks.html: You know that a difference of squares factors (Factoring Completely) but a sum of squares like $x^2 + 9$ does not. Cubes are different: both $a^3 - b^3$ and $a^3 + b^3$ factor.

$$a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2) \qquad a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$$ The binomial copies the sign in the middle of the original. The trinomial's middle term gets the opposite sign, and its last term is always $+b^2$.

Check by multiplying. $(a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$ $= a^3 + a^2b + ab^2 - a^2b - ab^2 - b^3$, and the four middle terms cancel in pairs, leaving $a^3 - b^3$. The middle sign has to be the opposite one, or those terms would double instead of cancel. Why must $a - b$ be a factor at all? Put $a = b$: then $a^3 - b^3 = 0$, so by the factor theorem (thinking of $a$ as the variable), $a - b$ divides it.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^3 - 8$ crosses the axis only at $x = 2$. Its factor $g(x) = x - 2$ gives that zero; the other factor $h(x) = x^2 + 2x + 4$ stays above the axis, which is why it doesn't factor further over the real numbers.

blocks.html: Copying the binomial's sign into the middle of the trinomial, as in $x^3 + 27 = (x + 3)(x^2 + 3x + 9)$. Multiply it out and you get $x^3 + 6x^2 + 18x + 27$, not $x^3 + 27$. The middle sign is always the opposite one. Also, the trinomial factor never factors further over the integers, so don't try.
